title: Prepositions of time
subtitle: during / in / over / throughout; until / by; so far
summary: Choose between during, in, over and throughout for periods of time, and between until, by, up to, until now and so far for the point where something stops.

lesson.heading: during and in
lesson.text: We use **during** or **in** for a period of time within which an event or activity happens. The activity may continue for the whole period, or it may happen once or several times inside it.

examples.text: I stayed at home **during** the summer.
The population of the city has actually fallen **during** the last decade.
We went to Turkey **during** the summer.
He suffered a number of injuries **during** his career as a jockey.

lesson.heading: during, not in
lesson.text: We use **during** rather than *in* to mean 'at some time in the period of' before nouns such as **illness, holiday, meal, stay, treatment** and **visit**, when we refer to an event that lasts some time. We also use during with **the whole (of)**.

examples.text: The President made the speech **during** a visit to Madrid.
No one was allowed to leave the ship **during the whole of** its time in port.

lesson.heading: throughout
lesson.text: We use **throughout** to emphasise that something happens over the whole of a period of time.

examples.text: We had enough firewood to keep us warm **throughout** the winter.

left.label: over or during - something that lasts a while
examples: Weather conditions have been improving **over** / **during** the past few days.
I hit my head and can't remember anything that happened **over** / **during** the next hour or so.

right.label: during only - a short event inside a period
examples: **During** a pause in the conversation, she left the room.

left.label: until (informally till) - continuing up to a time
examples: We have to be at home **until** 2:30.
= we must not leave home before 2:30

right.label: by - at that time at the latest
examples: We have to be at home **by** 2:30.
= we must arrive home either before or at 2:30

lesson.heading: up to and up till
lesson.text: In informal contexts we can use **up to** or **up till** instead of *until*. We commonly use them with **now** and **then**.

examples.text: I've just bought a tablet computer. I've always used a laptop **up to now**.

left.label: until now - the situation will not continue
examples: Supermarkets say that **until now** there has been little consumer interest in buying organic produce.
= the situation has changed or is going to change

right.label: so far / to date - it may well continue
examples: It was certainly the best match of the football season **so far**.
When the contract is signed it will be the building company's biggest order **to date**.

lesson.text: Until answers 'how long does it go on?'; by answers 'what is the deadline?'

exercises.prompt: I've got to pay the money back ___ the end of the month.
exercises.explanation: By gives a deadline: at the end of the month at the latest.

exercises.prompt: I've got ___ the end of the month to pay the money back.
exercises.explanation: Until measures the time that goes on up to that point.

exercises.prompt: Sorry I'm late. I've been in a meeting ___ now.
exercises.explanation: The meeting continued right up to the present moment.

exercises.prompt: She was already a leading economist ___ her early twenties.
exercises.explanation: By her early twenties = at that time at the latest.
She sneezed during the performance. A short event inside a period takes during, not over.

exercises.prompt: We had enough firewood to keep us warm ___ the winter.
exercises.explanation: Throughout stresses that it lasted the whole of the winter.

exercises.prompt: ___ the last three weeks we've covered thousands of kilometres by train.
exercises.explanation: The travelling lasted a long time inside the period, so either word works.

exercises.prompt: Incidentally, we bumped into your friend Eleni ___ our visit to the Van Gogh museum.
exercises.explanation: Before nouns like visit we use during rather than in.

exercises.prompt: ___ I thought Rome was the best city we'd been to, but I think I love Amsterdam even more.
exercises.explanation: The situation has changed, so until now is right.

exercises.prompt: We've been here for three days, and have been very impressed with what we've seen ___.
exercises.explanation: The visit is still going on, so we use so far, not until now.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to say that nobody could leave at any point in the whole period.
exercises.answer: No one was allowed to leave the ship during the whole of its time in port.
exercises.explanation: With the whole (of) we use during, never in.

exercises.prompt: Can the word in brackets replace during in each sentence?

items.text: The weather was terrible here during December. (in)
Do you think standards of numeracy have fallen during the last 20 years? (over)
My stomach ache got steadily worse during the evening. (over)
She lost more than 15 kilos during her illness. (in)
Karl had a phone call during the meal and had to leave early. (in)
People no longer expect to be employed in the same place during the whole of their working lives. (in)
He twisted his ankle during the match and had to retire injured. (over)
The meeting will be some time during January. (over)
